title: Inside an IBM Quantum Computer: Dilution Refrigerator Parts and Makers
content:
The gold "chandelier" most people picture as a quantum computer is actually a refrigerator. It is called a dilution refrigerator, and the real computer is a fingernail-sized chip hanging at the very bottom. IBM announced in August 2026 that it had linked two modular cryogenic systems and cooled them below 15 millikelvin, about −273°C. The cosmic microwave background is about −270°C, so the inside of this machine is colder than space.

1. Pulse-tube cooler — supplier not disclosed

The cylinder attached to the silver top plate does the first stage of cooling, taking the system from room temperature down to about −269°C. It works by compressing and expanding helium gas, the same principle as a household refrigerator or air conditioner. Getting colder than this takes a different method.

2. Dilution refrigerator — Bluefors and Oxford Instruments

The five gold plates are this section, and it is where the system reaches about −273°C. Mixing helium-3 and helium-4 separates them into two layers, and heat is absorbed when helium-3 crosses the boundary. No other known method reaches this temperature, so quantum computers around the world use the same approach. Bluefors and Oxford Instruments reportedly hold more than 70% of the dilution refrigerator market between them, and IBM Quantum System Two uses a Bluefors platform. Bluefors is not publicly listed, so the market leader cannot be bought. Oxford Instruments trades on the London Stock Exchange (LSE: OXIG).

3. Cryogenic RF wiring — supplier not disclosed

These are the thin lines running vertically between the plates. IBM's modular platform, announced in March 2026, contains more than 4,000 of them. More qubits need more wires, and every wire is also a path for heat to enter, which is one reason these machines are hard to scale.

In Korea, Sensorview (KOSDAQ: 321370) said in December 2025 that it made its first delivery of cryogenic, non-magnetic cables and connectors for quantum computers to a government-affiliated research institute. That delivery went to a Korean institute, not to IBM, and the company was reportedly still responding to a quote request from a U.S. company at that stage. (Reported)

4. Mixing chamber — helium-3 is a nuclear by-product

The copper cylinder at the bottom is the coldest point in the machine. Helium-3 is almost absent in nature; it comes from the decay of tritium, so in practice it is available only as a by-product of nuclear facilities. As more quantum computers are built, where to source it becomes a question.

5. Qubit chip — IBM

The black square mounted on the gold stage at the bottom is the actual computer. It is a superconducting circuit that IBM designs and manufactures itself (NYSE: IBM). Everything above it exists to cool and connect this one chip.

Why cool it this far?

Qubits lose their state with even tiny amounts of heat, so the large structure above exists to keep that single chip quiet. For reference, Japan's ULVAC said in March 2025 that it is working with IBM to develop a next-generation dilution refrigerator. IBM has never disclosed a price for Quantum System Two.

Quick FAQ

Is the gold machine in quantum computer photos the computer itself?
No. The gold structure is a dilution refrigerator. The computing happens on a fingernail-sized chip hanging at the bottom.

How cold does it get?
IBM said in August 2026 that it linked two modular cryogenic systems and cooled them below 15 millikelvin (IBM Newsroom, Aug 19, 2026), about −273°C, colder than the cosmic microwave background at about −270°C.

Can I invest in the company that makes the refrigerators?
The market leader, Bluefors, is not listed. Oxford Instruments is listed in London (LSE: OXIG).

Does a Korean-listed company supply IBM?
None is confirmed. Sensorview (KOSDAQ: 321370) said it delivered cryogenic cables and connectors to a Korean research institute, which is not an IBM delivery.

Companies named are disclosed or reported suppliers; parts with no confirmed supplier are labeled as such. Images are reconstructions, not an actual physical teardown.
